title: Socrates and His House
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from "Socrates and His House" in Fifty Famous Stories Retold by James Baldwin (1896), via Project Gutenberg. The syllable-break hyphen in the original edition's "Soc'ra-tes" has been corrected.
body: There once lived in Greece a very wise man whose name was Socrates. Young men from all parts of the land went to him to learn wisdom from him; and he said so many pleasant things, and said them in so delightful a way, that no one ever grew tired of listening to him.
One summer he built himself a house, but it was so small that his neighbors wondered how he could be content with it.
"What is the reason," said they, "that you, who are so great a man, should build such a little box as this for your dwelling house?"
"Indeed, there may be little reason," said he; "but, small as the place is, I shall think myself happy if I can fill even it with true friends."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who came from all parts of the land to see Socrates?
options: Merchants wanting to trade with him
Soldiers wanting him to lead their army
Young men wanting to learn wisdom from him
Kings wanting his advice on war

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why did no one ever grow tired of listening to Socrates?
options: He said pleasant things in a delightful way
He spoke only for a few minutes at a time
He paid his listeners for their attention
He always agreed with whatever they said

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does Socrates build for himself one summer?
options: A garden wall
A small boat
A schoolroom
A house

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what do the neighbors wonder about the house?
options: Why he built it so far from the city
How he could be content with something so small
Why it took him so long to finish it
How he afforded to build it at all

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what do the neighbors call the house when they question him?
options: "A house fit for a king"
"The strangest house in Greece"
"Such a little box as this"
"A house without a proper roof"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does Socrates say he hopes to fill his house with?
options: True friends
Fine furniture
Books and scrolls
Gold and silver

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why do the neighbors find the small house surprising?
options: They believe small houses are against the law in Greece
They think Socrates cannot afford anything larger
They assume he plans to move away soon
They expect a man of his reputation to live in something grander

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does Socrates's answer suggest he values more than the size of his home?
options: The cost of the materials used to build it
The true friendship of the people who might fill it
The number of rooms it can hold
The opinion his neighbors have of him

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "content" mean in "how he could be content with it"?
options: Wealthy
Proud
Satisfied
Ashamed

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the passage?
options: True friendship matters more to Socrates than the size of his house
Wise men should always live in the grandest houses available
Neighbors should never question how others choose to live
A small house is always a sign of poverty

options: Rome
Egypt
Persia
Greece

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did young men go to Socrates to learn?
options: Farming
Wisdom
Swordsmanship
Shipbuilding

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what season does Socrates build his house?
options: Winter
Spring
Summer
Autumn

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does Socrates's phrase "there may be little reason" suggest about his own view of the house's size?
options: He does not consider the house's small size worth arguing about
He secretly agrees the house is too small for him
He regrets not building a larger house

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might Socrates be untroubled by owning such a small house?
options: He plans to build a larger house very soon
He does not expect to live there for very long
He believes all houses in Greece are the same size
He measures a home's worth by the friendships within it, not its size

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "dwelling house" mean in the neighbors' question?
options: A house used only for storage
A house where someone lives
A house built for guests only
A house no longer in use

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: Socrates asks his neighbors to help him build a bigger house
Socrates is forced to sell his house due to its small size
Socrates explains that true friendship matters more to him than a grand house
Socrates argues with his neighbors over the cost of his house
